questions.stem: A model gives each of three must-do projects a bonus of $50,000k in its objective, with no must-do rows. After a budget cut, one of the three fits no year's budget in any start year. What does the solve return?

options.text: INFEASIBLE, since the bonus turns every must-do into a hard rule
options.says: A bonus is only an objective term; the weighted model has no row to break, so it still finds a plan.

options.text: OPTIMAL, with all three funded and that year's budget row exceeded
options.says: The budget rows still hold in every plan the solver returns; the weighted model meets them by dropping a must-do.

options.text: OPTIMAL, with that must-do dropped and every other bonus kept
options.says: Right: as with P017 after the cut, the weighted model drops the must-do that cannot fit and reports OPTIMAL.

options.text: UNBOUNDED, since a bonus that large has no limit in the objective
options.says: Each bonus multiplies a variable that is at most 1, so the objective is finite; the lesson's weighted run is OPTIMAL.

origin.section: A Must-Do Is an Equality Row, Not a Large Weight

questions.stem: A regulator rules that, of three substation rebuilds S1, S2 and S3, the plan must include one or more; which ones is the planner's choice. With started(i) for each rebuild, which rows state the rule?

options.says: Right: one counting row on the group, like underground_Ridge; any one rebuild meets it, and more are allowed.

options.text: Three rows: started(S) = 1 for each of S1, S2 and S3
options.says: That makes every member a must-do, the over-mandate that cost $273k in the undergrounding example.
An equality is "exactly one", the address row of an alternative group; it refuses a plan with two rebuilds, which the rule allows.
That is the alternative-group row; it allows a plan with no rebuild at all, which the rule forbids.

origin.section: A Group Can Be Mandated When No Single Project Is

questions.stem: Lifting mandate A alone raises the best plan's NPV by $300k; lifting mandate B alone raises it by $200k. Finance asks what A and B cost together. What do you report?

options.text: $500k, the sum of the two single costs
options.says: Single costs do not add: in the lesson they summed to $2,367k while the joint cost was $2,386k.

options.text: $300k, the larger of the two single costs
options.says: Nothing makes the joint cost the larger single cost; it has to be measured, and it can exceed the sum.

options.text: $100k, the gap between the two single costs
options.says: Shared budgets make the costs interact, but no rule turns that into a difference; only a solve gives the number.

options.text: The gain of one solve with both rows removed
options.says: Right: the joint cost is the best NPV without both rows less the best NPV with them, from one solve.

origin.section: The Cost of a Mandate Is the NPV You Give Up for It
